idiom_name: template compose(F, G) returning a capturing lambda
implementation_notes: Lambdas are anonymous callables and std::function<Out(In)> is the vocabulary type that can store them together with function pointers, bind expressions and function objects (cppreference), so a step is `auto normalize = [](std::string s) { ... };` and composition is a four-line template returning a capturing lambda. Nothing in the standard library is named compose, so this helper is the idiomatic replacement for the classic combinator; the type-erased std::function wrapper is still justified at stored boundaries where the concrete closure type must not leak into a header, while the raw auto-returning template is preferred for local chains because it inlines.
pitfalls: A lambda captures its steps by value at construction: rebuilding the chain per call pays the capture cost, and a step capturing by reference dangles if the chain outlives the referenced objects.
std::function erases the concrete closure type, may allocate for larger captures and blocks inlining; keep hot chains as auto and reserve std::function for stable, nameable boundaries.
The composed type is unnameable, so declaring such a chain in a header needs decltype gymnastics or a type-erased return - the point where the convenience ends.

variants.name: C++20 ranges adaptor pipeline (views::transform)
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 range adaptors compose lazily through the pipe operator: std::views::transform(f) and std::views::transform(g) are range adaptor closures, and applying them to a range yields a view that applies the steps per element only when iterated (cppreference: adaptors can be composed into pipelines). This is function composition in sequence shape - it keeps the ordering and reuse properties but not the scalar signature - so it is the right realization when the transformation is element-wise and laziness or the absence of intermediate containers matters; the lambda-compose variant stays the choice for scalar values and named reusable chains.
pitfalls: Adaptor closures are lazy: nothing executes until iteration, so side-effecting steps surprise callers who expect eager application.
views::transform is per element, so a chain that must collapse a sequence to one scalar needs a terminal step (ranges::fold_left, or ranges::to in C++23) instead of another adaptor.
Each adaptor adds an iterator/sentinel layer; deep pipelines can erase the type-level information needed for sized ranges or cheap random access.
